articles.title: If HC judgment is not stayed, all pillars will acquire religious character: Tamil Nadu govt tells Supreme Court
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Tamil Nadu government on Wednesday contended in the Supreme Court that permitting the lighting of the traditional Karthigai Deepam lamp atop a stone pillar, near the Dargah on Thiruparankundram hill, could lead to thousands of survey pillars across the country acquiring a religious character. Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, appearing for the Madurai District Collector, stated this before a bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi while seeking a stay on the Madras High Court's direction. Tamil Nadu urges Supreme Court to stay Madras HC order permitting lighting of traditional Karthigai Deepam "Our fear as a State is that if the judgment remains undisturbed, all these pillars will find religious colours and people will start doing these things... Let the court's jurisdiction not be expanded, otherwise thousands of survey pillars in the country will start becoming religious," Sankaranarayanan submitted. Senior advocate Huzefa Ahmadi, appearing for the Sikandar Badusha Auliya Dargah committee, contended that the single bench passed the order without giving adequate time to them to file a reply in accordance with the High Court rules. Ahmadi argued that the single judge of the High Court had conducted a site visit without notice to the Dargah before passing the order. The hearing will continue on Thursday. Seeking urgent interim relief, the state government had on Tuesday pointed out that the Karthigai Deepam festival, falling on November 24 this year, was approaching and that the lamp would have to be lit at the "disputed" location if the High Court's direction was not stayed. Senior advocate Jaideep Gupta, appearing for the state government, had said that there was no established custom of lighting the ceremonial lamp at the stone pillar, known as the Deepathoon. Earlier, the Tamil Nadu HR&CE Department had strongly opposed the petition seeking Archaeological Survey of India's (ASI) control over the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple and Thirupparankundram hill, and also changes in the traditional Karthigai Deepam celebrations. The Karthigai Deepam controversy at the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple at Madurai centres on a dispute over where and by whom the deepam should be lit on the Thirupparankundram hill. For decades, the deepam was lit at the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar temple on the lower slopes. Hindu groups had sought permission to light the lamp at the Deepathoon, an ancient stone lamp pillar located higher up the hill, approximately 50 metres away from the Hazrat Sultan Sikandar Badusha Auliya dargah. In an affidavit filed before the bench, the HR&CE Department opposed the plea which sought a direction to the ASI to take over the temple and the Thirupparankundram hill, saying the temple's ownership and the existing religious practices have been settled through decades of judicial proceedings. HR&CE Commissioner T G Vinay said the hill is owned by the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple, Thirupparankundram, to the extent recognised by a civil court decree of 1923, which was subsequently restored by the Privy Council in 1931. The affidavit opposed three reliefs sought by petitioner Hindu Dharma Parishad seeking the handing over of the entire temple and hill to the ASI, keeping a lamp burning round the clock at a stone pillar described as the Deepathoon and illuminating the entire hill with lamps during Karthigai Deepam. "A title so settled cannot be disturbed and the administration of a religious endowment entrusted by statute to the HR&CE cannot be wrested away and handed over to the ASI upon a petition that pleads no ground in law and seeks the relief in the teeth of a concluded civil adjudication of title," the affidavit said. On the contentious issue of lighting the Karthigai Deepam, the HR&CE commissioner maintained that the festival lamp has traditionally been lit at the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar temple and not at the hilltop or the stone pillar now being described as the Deepathoon. Madras HC order on lifting ban on supply of construction materials brings huge relief to Keralam It further referred to historical records of attempts made in 1862 and 1912 to light lamps near the summit of the hillock where the dargah is situated. Opposing the demand for an ASI takeover, the commissioner contended that archaeological protection at Thirupparankundram extends only to specified features, including the rock-cut cave and inscriptions, and not to the entire hill or the functioning temple. It cautioned that permitting lighting at multiple locations on the hill, particularly in the vicinity of the dargah, could disturb the existing arrangements and create law and order complications at a site with a history of communal tension.

articles.title: Uddhav Thackeray's decision to form MVA govt amounted to ideological departure, Eknath Shinde to Supreme Court
articles.summary: New Delhi: Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde faction told the Supreme Court on Wednesday that the decision of the Uddhav Thackeray-led leadership to sever ties with the BJP and form the Maha Vikas Aghadi government in November 2019 with the Congress and the NCP was a departure from the ideological platform on which the Shiv Sena had sought votes. A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was told by senior advocate Dhruv Mehta, appearing for the Shinde faction, that the legislators who dissented against Thackeray in June 2022 did not abandon the Shiv Sena but were seeking to restore the party's original ideological identity and political alignment. Dissent not defection: Shinde faction to Supreme Court over Shiv Sena row "It is concluded, as also rightly held by the Hon'ble speaker, that the Tenth Schedule is not a device for imposing intra-party discipline or for administering the party." "It was further observed that no party leadership may use its provisions to stifle collective dissent among a large number of members by threatening disqualification, and that a tussle for leadership between rival leaders is a matter for the party itself, not one in which the speaker has any role to play," Mehta said while concluding his arguments in the case. He sought to place the rebellion in the context of the political developments following the 2019 Maharashtra assembly elections. He said the Shiv Sena contested the elections in a pre-poll alliance with the BJP, securing 56 seats, while the BJP won 105 seats. The alliance had a combined strength of 161 in the 288-member Assembly, he said. He alleged that the subsequent decision of Thackeray to sever ties with the BJP and form the MVA government with the Congress and the NCP did not go down well with cadres on the ground. According to the Shinde faction, the change in political alignment caused considerable resentment among party workers and legislators, who felt that the party had moved away from the Hindutva ideology associated with its founder Balasaheb Thackeray. "This is not a matter of sentiment but of constitutional significance. As already submitted, the electoral mandate is obtained in the name of the political party, upon its symbol and upon the platform it places before the electorate… Ideology, in the scheme of the Tenth Schedule, is therefore not a peripheral consideration. It is the content of the mandate which the Schedule exists to protect," he said. It was not a mandate for a government of the Shiv Sena with the Congress and the NCP, the parties against which the Shiv Sena had contested and campaigned, he said. "For nearly two-and-a-half years, the Shiv Sainik on the ground was required to defend an alliance with those he had been asked, months earlier, to oppose. This shift also started reflecting in the party ideology and functioning." "Shiv Sainiks working at ground level, at the constituency level and were confronted daily with the resentment of their own workers over a different functioning. articles.title: Karnataka HC stays probes against ten BJP BLAs accused of attempting voter deletions
articles.summary: The Karnataka High Court has stayed further investigation in three FIRs against ten BJP Booth Level Agents (BLAs) accused of filing bulk Form 7 objections to delete voters' names. The latest interim orders take the number of cases in which police probes have been stayed over the allegations to five. Justice Anant Ramnath Hegde passed the orders on November 17, in petitions filed by the booth agents. The cases concern complaints from Mysuru, Jayanagar in Bengaluru and Kodagu, alleging that incorrect information was submitted in applications seeking deletion of voters from electoral rolls during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). The three FIRs name Harish Kumar C, M Raghavendra and Anil Thomas in the Mysuru case; Ramakrishna and Yogesh DR in the Bengaluru case; and UH Lokesh, Rajini, Nagaraj AC, Savitha N Malali and Basavaraju BN in the Kodagu case. The petitioners face charges under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including section 319, which deals with impersonation, section 336 on forgery and section 61(2) on criminal conspiracy. The complaints allege that false information was submitted through Form 7 applications seeking the deletion of voters from electoral rolls. Some complaints in the wider set of cases alleged that Muslim voters were being targeted. The court had earlier, on October 9, stayed further investigation in two other FIRs against BJP booth agents G S Vasanthalakshmi and Deepak Singh R. The latest orders extend the interim protection to the three additional cases. Form 7 is used to object to the inclusion of a name in the electoral roll or seek the deletion of an existing entry based on certain criteria. Under the Registration of Electors Rules (1960), the Electoral Registration Officer is required to examine such objections, conduct an inquiry where necessary and give affected persons an opportunity to be heard before deciding on deletion. The court observed that this statutory process should be carried out before the question of police investigation is considered. It said the election authorities are empowered to examine the correctness of information submitted in Form 7 and take action if false declarations are established. “The statutory scheme under the Registration of Electors Rules provides for scrutiny and inquiry into the correctness of the information furnished under Form No.7 and penal consequences in case of false information,” the court said. It also noted that differences in signatures on Form 7 applications, by themselves, would not establish forgery. The Electoral Registration Officer must verify whether the person named in an application had signed it. If the person denies having done so, further inquiry may be necessary, the court said. The court said voters whose names are proposed to be deleted must also be given an opportunity to be heard. It directed the Election Commission to place on record the material relating to the decisions taken on the Form 7 applications and asked that it be impleaded as a respondent. Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, provides for punishment for knowingly making a false declaration in connection with electoral rolls. The offence is punishable with imprisonment of up to one year, a fine, or both. The court said the complainants could seek modification or vacation of its orders. The state government may also seek modification after the relevant records are placed before the court.

articles.title: K Balanchander classics restored, to premiere in France
articles.summary: Acclaimed filmmaker K Balachander’s films Achamillai Achamillai , Aval Oru Thodarkathai and Thanneer Thanneer were restored by Prasad Corp, one of India’s well-known restoration and post-production facilities. The restoration was a part of the National Film Heritage Mission (NFHM), according to a press statement. The NHFM is an initiative of the National Film Archive of India (NFAI), aimed at preserving India's cinematic heritage. Dayal Padmanabhan returns to Kannada cinema after 3-year hiatus with 'Nari Kathe' The three restored films will be screened at the 48th edition of Festival des 3 Continents, between November 20 and 28 in Nantes, France. The films will be screened as a part of a special programme titled ‘Kailasam Balachander, Society in the Spotlight (India)’. The programme will also feature Sindhu Bhairavi , Rudra Veena , Nizhal Nijamakirathu and Maro Charithra . The three restored works showcase Balachander’s focus on sharp social issues, political critique, and complex human conditions. The films are also known for their strong women characters who navigate difficult societal, economic and moral realities. In Achamillai Achamillai , a sharp satire on the Indian political system, for example, Saritha’s character Thenmozhi is considered as one of the strongest and most iconic female characters in Indian cinema. Thanneer Thanneer examines caste dynamics, religious superstition and systemic exploitation in a drought-stricken remote village suffering from severe shortage of drinking water. And Aval Oru Thodarkathai (She is a never-ending story) explores a hardworking middle-class woman who is the sole breadwinner for her large, dependent, and ungrateful family. Prasad Corp undertook digital restoration, colour grading, digital mastering and French subtitling, for their screenings at the festival. “The process brought renewed visual clarity to these cinematic works while retaining their original visual character and creative intent,” the press note said. Prasad Corp was founded in 1956 by legendary filmmaker L V Prasad.

articles.title: The Rise of Predictive Living: How AI Is Changing the Way We Plan Our Future Money
articles.summary: The growing preference for anticipating future outcomes is now finding its way into financial planning , where artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies are changing how individuals understand, monitor and manage their money. Consider a working professional who begins the month with a salary credit, regular household expenses, loan repayments, subscriptions and investments. Earlier, keeping track of these financial commitments largely depended on maintaining spreadsheets, checking bank statements or manually calculating monthly expenses. Today, digital financial tools can help categorise transactions, identify recurring spending patterns, highlight unusual expenses and, where supported, provide estimates of future account balances. Some platforms also use predictive analytics to help users understand how their spending behaviour could influence their financial position over the coming weeks. Rather than simply presenting a record of past transactions, technology is gradually making financial information more forward-looking. This shift towards anticipating rather than merely reacting to financial situations can be understood through the idea of predictive living. It is not necessarily about predicting every financial outcome accurately, but about using available information to make better-informed decisions. A monthly cash-flow forecast may help someone avoid overspending, but it cannot independently answer whether they are financially prepared for their child's higher education fifteen years from now, a retirement that may be decades away or other significant milestones that require sustained financial commitment. This is where the distinction between short-term financial visibility and long-term financial preparedness becomes important. This is where savings-oriented life insurance plans such as HDFC Life Click 2 Achieve (C2A) (UIN: 101N186V09) a Non-Linked, Non-Participating, Individual Savings Life Insurance Plan can play a role. Rather than a single fixed format, the plan can be shaped around when and how the money is needed. A parent saving for higher education, for instance, can have payouts begin as the child turns 16 or 18 and spread across the years when fees fall due. Someone working towards a milestone on a fixed date can opt for a guaranteed lump sum, while someone thinking about later life can choose a regular income instead. Throughout, the plan carries life cover, so the family's goals stay on track even if circumstances change. In that sense, the two approaches work together rather than in place of each other. Technology helps people understand their present financial behaviour and see near-term cash flows clearly. Structured planning turns that awareness into commitments towards milestones that lie years ahead. One shows where money is going; the other shapes where it can take you. Predictive living, therefore, is not simply about knowing what tomorrow's bank balance might look like. It is about developing the confidence to make decisions today with a better understanding of tomorrow's possibilities. As AI continues to influence how people interact with money, combining digital visibility with disciplined long-term financial planning could become an increasingly important part of building financial confidence. After all, the most meaningful financial prediction is not necessarily knowing exactly what the future holds, but being better prepared for it. articles.summary: Mendhar: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Wednesday attacked the BJP-led Centre over the denial of statehood to Jammu and Kashmir and wondered whether the party was deliberately deferring it till gets its own chief minister in the Union Territory. Abdullah said the repeated promise of statehood at an "appropriate time" has become meaningless. "If it is your wish not to restore statehood until the BJP has its own chief minister in Jammu and Kashmir, then say it openly. Tell the people clearly so that they are not kept under any illusion, and we are not humiliated repeatedly," he said, addressing a public rally in Mendhar township of Poonch district. Omar Abdullah’s two years: Will Delhi restore statehood, and on what terms? Omar Abdullah reiterates demand to restore Jammu & Kashmir’s statehood on PM Modi’s birthday The chief minister said it is more than two years since his government assumed office, but the Centre has yet to honour its commitment to restore statehood, which it had promised would be done after delimitation and the assembly election. "Even after waiting for two years and one month, we have been compelled to ask: Where has our state gone? Why is the restoration of statehood being delayed?" he asked. On the Centre's "appropriate time" deadline, Abdullah said, "What is the yardstick you have to measure this? What kind of scale will you use to decide that the time has finally come to restore our statehood?" He also accused the central dispensation of using security incidents to justify the continued delay, even though the elected government has no control over the police or law and order. Referring to the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack and several terror incidents in Kulgam, Reasi, and Kishtwar over the past two years, the chief minister said the elected government is being made to account for failures in areas outside its jurisdiction. "We have no control over the police or law and order, yet we are told that because of the Pahalgam attack, perhaps statehood cannot be restored now. An incident takes place in Kulgam, and the same justification is given. An attack takes place in Reasi or Kishtwar, and again the same argument is put forward," he said. "How can you hold us responsible for matters over which we have no control? We have fulfilled our responsibilities in the areas entrusted to us. Why should the people of Jammu and Kashmir suffer for the failures of others? What kind of justice is this?" the National Conference leader added. Abdullah challenged the Centre to assess his government on infrastructure, healthcare, education and governance, rather than law and order, which is beyond its remit. "Either your intentions are not right, or you are not being sincere. If you do not want to restore statehood until the BJP gets its own chief minister, then have the courage to say so," he said. The chief minister also accused the Centre of deliberately reducing the standing of elected representatives by continuing the Union Territory arrangement. Pointing to protocol differences, Abdullah said the chief secretaries and chief justices enjoyed comparable status, but the chief ministers, ministers and MLAs of Union Territories are placed below their counterparts in states. "You do not want to weaken the chief secretary or undermine the chief justice. You want to weaken the people's elected government and humiliate their elected representatives," he said. Recalling the Centre's assurances before the Supreme Court during the proceedings concerning Article 370, he said the commitment was to restore statehood after delimitation, elections and the formation of an elected government. Abdullah said his government passed a resolution seeking restoration of statehood in its very first Cabinet meeting, and he personally submitted it to Prime Minister Narendra Modi. He said he has repeatedly reminded the prime minister of the commitment whenever he visited Jammu and Kashmir, including during the inauguration of the Sonamarg Tunnel and the Katra railway project, and also with Union Home Minister Amit Shah in Delhi. Despite the limitations, Abdullah said, his government neither used its restricted powers as an excuse nor backed away from its responsibilities. "We are not cowards who get frightened by difficult situations or use them as an excuse for our inability to deliver," he said.

articles.title: Trump's Board of Peace faults Israel and Hamas for failure to end Gaza war
articles.summary: Jerusalem: The body overseeing US President Donald Trump's plan to end the Gaza war accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to meet their commitments to end hostilities, leaving the population of Gaza in dire conditions and the ceasefire in danger of collapse. The 12-page Board of Peace report, seen by Reuters, is the body's second to the United Nations Security Council since the US-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a sobering assessment of progress made since then. Explained | Trump's Gaza plan hinges on Hamas disarmament, Israeli withdrawals The board, established and headed by Trump, is expected to present the report's findings to a meeting of the council in New York at the end of November. "The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process," the report said, warning that "a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely." The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and a spokesperson for the political office of Hamas did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the report. Peace plan stalled While the ceasefire has halted major fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect last year. Hamas agreed in July to a Board of Peace roadmap to surrender its weapons and transfer governance of Gaza to a civilian transitional authority, but Israel rejected the roadmap, saying it will not withdraw until Hamas is dismantled. Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza, while the report said Hamas fighters have also continued attacks on Israeli troops. "Every day that Israel continues strikes against Hamas targets, it delays putting Hamas' agreement to the roadmap to the test," the report said. "Meanwhile, Hamas militant activity continues, the commitment to cease all military activities has not been met in full by the parties, and the population faces another winter in tents and rubble." Israeli 'absence of decisions' Gaza's population of more than 2 million Palestinians lives confined to around a third of the coastal territory, mostly in makeshift tents and damaged buildings, under the control of Hamas fighters. Israel occupies two-thirds of Gaza that has been largely razed and depopulated. The report criticised Israel's government for an "absence of decisions" on arrangements to train and deploy a civilian Palestinian police force to replace Hamas as Gaza's law enforcement authority. It said this was impeding the full implementation of the plan. It said restrictions imposed by Israel on supplies and equipment, alongside funding shortfalls, had hindered the ability of Gazans to prepare for and respond to seasonal flooding. Heavy rain inundated displacement camps last week across Gaza and more rain is expected later this month. Hamas, for its part, was collecting taxes on goods entering Gaza that were impacting the availability of basic commodities, the report said. The Board of Peace was established by Trump to oversee his ambitious plan to end the war that Israel launched in response to Hamas-led attacks from Gaza in October 2023. Israel PM Netanyahu rejects Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza Around 1,200 people were killed in Israel in the 2023 Hamas attacks, while the Israeli assault on Gaza has since killed 74,000 Palestinians. More than 1,600 Palestinians, including many civilians, and five Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the US-mediated ceasefire was struck in October 2025. Trump's plan received strong international backing, though the board itself has been met with scepticism from many of Washington's Western allies. Netanyahu's right-wing coalition government remains in power in Israel in a caretaker capacity despite losing its majority in an inconclusive election last month. On Wednesday, Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel would not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas was dismantled and Gaza was demilitarized.

articles.title: Trump administration weighs forcing US firms to disclose Chinese AI use: Report
articles.summary: Washington: The Trump administration is considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, a bid to discourage reliance on the technology without imposing new restrictions that could anger industry or Beijing , three people told Reuters . The Treasury Department and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) have discussed the plan, which would apply to companies such as Airbnb, the people said. The company uses Qwen, an AI model made by China's Alibaba, to power its AI customer service agent. Under the plan, companies like Airbnb would be required to post that information on their websites. It was not immediately clear if the idea was gaining traction within the administration or if it would be enshrined in a formal rulemaking process if it does move forward. But its consideration, first reported by Reuters, underscores an emerging push within the administration toward combating the spread of powerful Chinese open weight models, a source of deep concern within the government. Open weight models make their core components publicly available for anyone to download and adapt. The proposal also shows officials are looking at ways to discourage use of Chinese AI through a "name and shame" campaign while sticking to a broader anti-regulation stance on AI. The White House, the Treasury Department, Alibaba, and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Airbnb declined to comment. The consideration comes as revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy have fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China. They have turned a spotlight on cases of ​Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats. Chinese-made open-weight models are gaining ground with US companies because they are cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic, and perform well enough. But China hawks fear Beijing is using such models — like Moonshot AI's Kimi, DeepSeek or Qwen — to hook US companies so they will become dependent on Chinese AI. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in July that the Trump administration could sanction Chinese AI companies if they were found to be guilty of intellectual property theft via distillation of American models. Senator accuses US Commerce Department of failing to stem flow of AI chips to China Distillation is the process of training smaller ​AI models ⁠using the output of larger ones as part of an effort to lower the costs of training a powerful new AI tool. Bessent's remarks echoed comments in April by Michael Kratsios, OSTP director, who accused China of stealing US artificial ​intelligence labs' intellectual property on an "industrial scale," spurring a State Department-led push to highlight such behavior to foreign counterparts. Congressional investigation But US officials have stopped short of restricting or taking punitive action against Chinese AI companies. The issue has attracted the attention of Congress. Republican US Representatives Andrew Garbarino of New York and John Moolenaar of Michigan, who chair the House Homeland Security Committee and the House select committee on China, respectively, launched an investigation into American companies' use of Chinese AI this year. They sent letters to Airbnb as well as Anysphere, the maker of the AI coding tool Cursor, whose Composer 2 AI model was built on a version of Kimi. A letter was also sent to DoorDash , whose co-founder said the company routes some tasks in an internal system through Kimi. Moonshot, DoorDash, and SpaceX, which bought Anysphere, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Chinese AI models were the three most popular by token usage in October on OpenRouter, an AI marketplace platform that tracks usage data. Tokens are units of data processed by AI models. Chinese AI models have even been used by the US government itself. Reuters reported in September that a US government website deployed an AI model from China's Alibaba to allow users to search proposed federal regulations even though the FBI accused the model's developer of copying Anthropic's technology. American open-weight models include Meta's Muse Glimmer, Nvidia's Nemotron and Reflection AI's Beam.

articles.title: India unveils 1st homegrown H5N1 vaccine to combat bird flu amid rising outbreaks
articles.summary: In an effort to strengthen India’s preparedness for controlling outbreaks caused by highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), the country is launching its first indigenously developed vaccine against the H5N1 bird flu virus. Developed by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) and the National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), the inactivated vaccine will target the H5N1 virus belonging to Clade 2.3.2.1a. This strain is linked to several bird flu outbreaks in chickens in India. In recent times, infections caused by this strain have also been detected in different animal species, including mammals, along with three human cases. This makes it important to control the spread of this virus to reduce financial losses for poultry farmers and prevent its transmission from chickens to other animals and humans. The vaccine is expected to protect against H5N1 strains of this clade circulating in India. At present, there is no specific commercially available vaccine in India providing protection against the Clade 2.3.2.1a H5N1 virus strain. Therefore, this discovery is crucial for the ountry. The impact of bird flu is not limited to poultry farms. Outbreaks can cause nearly 100 per cent mortality among infected birds, leading to major financial losses . Moreover, it also affects global trade, prices of poultry products and the livelihoods of farmers. For instance, the 2006 bird flu outbreak caused estimated direct and indirect losses of Rs. 2,200–3,000 crore. The disease is also a public health concern. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), 1,003 human cases of H5N1 avian influenza, including 479 deaths, have been reported across 25 countries, including India, since 2003. Studies have shown that the H5N1 strain known as Clade 2.3.2.1a has been responsible for most bird flu outbreaks in chickens. Recently, infections caused by this strain have also been detected in other animal species, including mammals, as well as three human cases. This makes it important to control the spread of this virus to reduce financial losses for poultry farmers and prevent its transmission from chickens to other animals and humans.

articles.title: Goldman Sachs predicts RBI may hike interest rates by 75 basis points by Q2 2027
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may raise the benchmark interest rate by 75 basis points by the second quarter of calendar year 2027, as rising food prices and broadening inflationary pressures are likely to prompt monetary tightening, according to a Goldman Sachs Research report. The interest rate hike is expected to moderate India's real GDP growth to 7.2 per cent in CY27, down from an estimated 7.9 per cent in CY26. Goldman Sachs expects the RBI to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points in December, followed by another 50 basis points in the first half of CY27, taking the rate to 6.25 per cent by Q2 CY27, the report said. "With headline inflation likely to remain slightly above 6 per cent through Q4 CY26 and Q1 CY27 in our forecasts, and price pressures broadening across core goods and services, we expect the RBI to continue its 'calibrated tightening' cycle," the report said. Inflation breaches RBI red line of 6% as food prices soar The RBI raised its benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent in the October policy, its first hike in nearly four years. Goldman Sachs expects India's headline retail inflation to average 5.7 per cent in CY27, while core inflation is projected at 4.7 per cent, driven by higher food prices, weather disruptions associated with El Nino and elevated input costs. Goldman Sachs Chief India Economist Santanu Sengupta said inflation has already breached the upper end of the RBI's target band, reaching 6.1 per cent in October. He expects inflation to remain around 6 per cent over the next two quarters before gradually easing towards the early 5 per cent range by the end of the year. Despite the anticipated monetary tightening, Goldman Sachs expects India's real GDP growth to remain robust at 7.2 per cent in CY27, moderating from an estimated 7.9 per cent in CY26. The report said strong domestic demand, resilient private consumption and an emerging investment cycle in energy, materials and strategic manufacturing sectors would continue to support economic activity. However, tighter financial conditions, higher corporate borrowing costs and fading effects of tax cuts could weigh on consumption and investment growth. Goldman Sachs projected real investment growth at around 8.5 per cent in CY27, supported by sectors aligned with India's energy security, defence and supply-chain priorities. On the external front, the current account deficit is expected to remain contained at around 1 per cent of GDP in CY26 and CY27, supported by robust services exports and remittances. Goldman Sachs raises India’s 2026 GDP growth forecast to 6.8% The report also forecast the rupee at 94, 95 and 96 against the US dollar over the next three, six and 12 months, respectively. On the Union Budget 2027-28, Sengupta said,"the underlying fiscal consolidation or sticking to that path will continue. I think the expenditure allocation towards capex also sort of remains constant as a share of GDP". Goldman Sachs upgraded India to 'overweight' and set a Nifty target of 28,500 by end-2027, citing expected mid-teen earnings growth, strong domestic demand and relatively low foreign investor positioning. It said India remains an attractive destination for investors seeking diversification amid global artificial intelligence-related market uncertainties.

articles.title: 'I didn't give a complete and truthful account; not just three, but whole team knew about it' | Cameron Bancroft opens up on sandpapergate
articles.summary: The sandpaper scam of 2018 took a further twist with Australia's Cameron Bancroft claiming the entire team knew about their ball-tampering plot that rocked cricket, directly contradicting current captain Pat Cummins. Recently, retired batter Usman Khawaja reignited the 'sandpapergate' scandal in his autobiography, alleging the whole team was in the know, and he was strongly backed by David Warner. Pat Cummins threw Usman Khawaja under the bus: David Warner says sandpaper allegations are true A Cricket Australia probe concluded only then-skipper Steve Smith, his deputy Warner and Bancroft were responsible for using sandpaper to rough up the ball in the third Test at Cape Town. They were all sent home in disgrace and banned. Cummins however said Khawaja was '100 per cent wrong' in a lengthy press conference on the issue. Breaking his silence, Bancroft wrote in a 4,000-word column, first published in The West Australian ,: "It wasn't just the three of us -- Steve Smith, David Warner and I -- who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team. "When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation I didn't give a complete and truthful account. "I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for and the involvement and awareness of others. "I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me." Bancroft said the release of Khawaja's book and Cummins' strenuous denials had forced him to come clean. Usman Khawaja's 'Sabr' claims revive ghosts of sandpaper scandal "The recent release of Usman Khawaja's autobiography, Sabr, has brought many of those memories back to the surface," he said. "It was freeing to hear on a personal level the truth of the chronology of events finally out there, a burden I have carried all these years. "But the final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference. "It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone. "What I saw, experienced and lived with -- not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa -- is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time," added Bancroft, whose international career was the worst affected of the trio involved in the scandal with the 33-year-old making only two more appearances after the controversial Test series against South Africa. (With inputs from agencies)

articles.title: Carpenter, college dropout: LeT commander Lateef Bhat killed in Kulgam encounter, a year after picking up gun
articles.summary: Security forces on Wednesday gunned down Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kulgam district. He got killed right after one year to the day he is believed to have picked up the gun to become one of the Valley’s most wanted terrorists. Kashmir’s last identified active local militant, Lateef Bhat, refuses surrender offer, killed in Kulgam encounter A former carpenter, Bhat finished his Class 12 in 2021 and dropped out of college soon after. He went missing in November last year and joined LeT and its offshoot, The Resistance Front (TRF), officials said. According to the police, Bhat, who was in his 20s, was responsible for the attack on a CRPF post in south Kashmir’s Kulgam area on November 11. He was trapped inside a mosque, a week later, refusing repeated appeals to surrender made by senior police and Army officers via video calls. The boy from Khrewan area in Kulgam refused. The Army subsequently used teargas to flush him out of hiding and gunned him down. The cycle of violence that began on November 18, 2025 had ended exactly a year later. "I do not think there is a bigger success than this in 2026," Superintendent of Police (SSP), Kulgam, Anayat Ali Chowdhary told reporters. Terming the operation a major success, he said Bhat was heavily self-radicalised. "After joining the banned organisation Lashkar-e-Taiba, he was receiving directions from across (the border) to disrupt peace here, hit tourism, and damage the economy. You have all seen his three or four attacks and how ruthlessly he carried them out," the SSP added. Bhat had managed to give security forces the slip a few times in the past "but was trapped very effectively this time", he said. He is suspected to have killed a policeman in Anantnag on July 22, 2026 and is the prime suspect in the targeted killing of two non-local labourers from Chhattisgarh in Kulgam a few days later on July 31. Unidentified terrorist killed in Kulgam encounter, search on for LeT’s Lateef Bhat Security agencies had put a reward of Rs 15 lakh for his capture. He leaves behind his parents, a brother and a married sister. (With agency inputs)

articles.title: SpiceJet board approves Rs 5,500 crore fund raising proposal
articles.summary: New Delhi: Struggling SpiceJet 's board on Wednesday approved a proposal to raise up to Rs 5,500 crore to shore up its financial position. The airline has been facing multiple headwinds, including financial and operational woes. At its meeting on Wednesday, the airline's board was apprised of investment discussions with potential new investors. The board has cleared the proposal to raise up to Rs 5,500 crore to strengthen the airline's financial position, rebuild capacity and drive its revival, according to a statement. Further, the board has directed the management to work towards closing it expeditiously. "The proposed fundraise may be undertaken through a combination of equity and other permitted instruments and will be subject to the requisite approvals," the statement said. Besides, the board has approved increasing the company's authorised share capital from Rs 2,000 crore to Rs 7,500 crore, subject to the necessary shareholder and regulatory approvals. The airline said it has been operating in an exceptionally challenging environment, with geopolitical disturbances and airspace restrictions putting pressure on operations. 'No flights took off from 7 pm yesterday': Severe disruptions in SpiceJet flights leave passengers stranded in Mumbai airport "This has been compounded by a sharp rise in aviation turbine fuel prices, which have more than doubled over the past few months, significantly increasing the cost of operations," it said. According to SpiceJet, the proposed fundraise is expected to provide the airline with the financial headroom to address these challenges, strengthen its balance sheet, support its fleet expansion and meet its operational requirements. "It will also support the airline's efforts to restore its network and build a stronger, more sustainable business," the statement said. SpiceJet Chairman and Managing Director Ajay Singh said the fundraise will provide an important opportunity to rebuild the airline, strengthen its operations and restore the brand. Shares of SpiceJet rose nearly 5 per cent to Rs 9.97 apiece in late afternoon trade on the BSE. The airline's domestic market share dropped to 0.6 per cent in September from 1.2 per cent in August, according to the latest DGCA data.

articles.title: Karnataka aims to become India’s Quantum Capital, government invites partnerships with US companies
articles.summary: Bengaluru: Karnataka is working towards positioning Bengaluru as the quantum capital of India and is keen to build strong partnerships with U.S. companies, universities and research institutions through the proposed Quantum City , said Dr. Ajay Dharam Singh, Minister for Minor Irrigation and Science & Technology. Speaking at the session on U.S.–India Collaboration: Cracking Quantum Code Together, organised as part of the USIBC India–U.S. Tech Conclave at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, the Minister invited American quantum technology companies to explore Karnataka as a destination for research, innovation, investment and technology development. ಕ್ವಾಂಟಮ್ ತಂತ್ರಜ್ಞಾನದಿಂದ ಜಲ ನಿರ್ವಹಣೆಯವರೆಗೆ – ಕರ್ನಾಟಕದ ಸಂಶೋಧನೆಗೆ ಜಾಗತಿಕ ಸಹಭಾಗಿತ್ವದ ಬಲ! ಬೆಂಗಳೂರು ಟೆಕ್ ಸಮ್ಮಿಟ್–2026ರ ಅಂಗವಾಗಿ ಇಸ್ರೇಲ್‌ನ ಡೀಪ್‌ಟೆಕ್ ಕ್ಷೇತ್ರದ ಪ್ರತಿನಿಧಿಗಳೊಂದಿಗೆ ಸಂವಾದ ನಡೆಸಿ, ಕ್ವಾಂಟಮ್ ಕಂಪ್ಯೂಟಿಂಗ್, ಕೃತಕ ಬುದ್ಧಿಮತ್ತೆ ಆಧಾರಿತ ಜಲ ನಿರ್ವಹಣೆ ಹಾಗೂ ಸುಧಾರಿತ ತಂತ್ರಜ್ಞಾನ ಕ್ಷೇತ್ರಗಳಲ್ಲಿ… pic.twitter.com/VeXYe96uc5 — Dr. Ajay Dharam Singh / ಡಾ. ಅಜಯ ಸಿಂಗ್ (@ajaydharamsingh) November 17, 2026 “Our ambition is clear — Karnataka should emerge as India’s quantum capital and Bengaluru should become a global destination for quantum technologies. I invite U.S. companies, universities and research institutions to partner with us in building Quantum City and the larger quantum ecosystem in Karnataka,” Dr. Ajay Dharam Singh said. He said Quantum City is being envisioned not merely as a physical infrastructure project, but as an integrated ecosystem connecting research institutions, startups, industry, investors, talent and global technology partners. Karnataka to strengthen research collaboration with Israel The proposed ecosystem will aim to provide startups and researchers access to shared laboratories, specialised equipment, testing facilities and advanced quantum infrastructure, reducing the high entry barriers associated with quantum technology development. “Quantum technologies require capital-intensive infrastructure which individual startups cannot always create on their own. Our approach is to develop shared facilities where researchers, startups and companies can access the infrastructure needed to move from research to prototype and from prototype to commercialisation,” the Minister said. Dedicated Quantum Technology Policy Dr. Singh said Karnataka is also moving towards a comprehensive Quantum Technology Policy covering research support, academic institutions, startups, industry participation, investment incentives, international partnerships, funding mechanisms and measurable implementation targets. The State’s Quantum Task Force recently reviewed the policy framework and the next phase of the Quantum City project. He stressed that the U.S.–India partnership could play an important role in areas such as quantum computing, communication, sensing, cybersecurity, hardware, talent development and commercialisation of research. Karnataka aims to emerge as global hub for AI, deep tech and semiconductor manufacturing: CM DK Shivakumar at Bengaluru Tech Summit “The next phase of quantum technology cannot be built in isolation. It requires collaboration across countries, universities, industries and startups. Karnataka wants Quantum City to become a platform where Indian and U.S. innovators can jointly develop technologies, test solutions and create products for global markets,” he said. The Minister said Bengaluru’s strong base of scientific institutions, engineering talent, technology companies and startups provides Karnataka with a natural advantage in building a globally competitive quantum ecosystem. “We want the journey to be clear — from research to innovation, innovation to enterprise and enterprise to global scale. articles.summary: The Inside Deutsche Bank leak was obtained by Indian author and journalist, Josy Joseph, and South African investigative journalist, Khadija Sharife. The investigation was coordinated by Barracuda Media in South Africa, with technical support from the Data and Research Center (DARC) in Germany. As the world eased into the new year in January 2022, a committee at Deutsche Bank headquarters in Frankfurt prepared to discuss if the bank should go ahead with deals which could hurt its reputation. On its agenda for the Jan. 12 meeting was EUR 11.4 million euros advance payment guarantee to German defence manufacturer Renk GmbH, to fund a contract with the Israel Ministry of Defence that would continue until 2027. Renk was to make gearboxes for its Merkava 4 tanks, with the first of the products to be delivered in September 2024. A document weighing up the deal had been on the tables of Deutsche Bank’s decision makers since Dec 16, 2021. An assistant general counsel for the bank was among those who contributed his views. He thought the deal involved a “plain vanilla trade finance product which does not carry any remarkable RepRisk in itself.” He said the likelihood of the deal becoming public was “very low”. But the risk would be even lower if the financing guarantees could be made via an Israeli bank on Deutsche Bank’s behalf, he said. The gearboxes, he added, were not considered weapons under the German Military Weapons Act, and Renk will secure a license to export them. “I am supportive of the transaction,” he said. The deal went ahead. Merkava 4 against civilians Two years later, in January 2024, six-year-old Palestinian Hind Rajab was on the phone to emergency services, pleading to be rescued. Rajab and six family members were fleeing Israeli attacks in Gaza when the car they were travelling in was shot at. By that point, she was the only one still alive. After hours of negotiation for safe passage, an ambulance crew heading to rescue the preschooler was intercepted. It would be days before the bodies of the first responders, Hind and her family could be reached. A total of 335 bullet holes were found on the family’s car. The Israeli government initially said none of its forces were present, and later claimed the bullet holes came from crossfire. However, satellite imagery and audio analysis of the incident by Forensic Architecture, a research group at Goldsmiths, University of London, found only the presence of the Israeli Defence Force (IDF) at the scene. In an October 2025 filing to the International Criminal Court, the Hind Rajab Foundation alleged that the tanks were Merkava 4. A tank round was found among the remains of the ambulance crew that had attempted to rescue Rajab. Initially, the IDF denied being in the area at the time, then said it "conducted raids on terror targets" in the neighbourhood. On Aug 19, 2026, more than two years after the incident, the IDF confirmed that its soldiers had opened fire on the car Rajab had been in, as well as at the rescue ambulance. It blamed the shooting on “failures in the co-ordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent Society ambulance, a claim the PRCS refuted. The IDF said a criminal investigation would be undertaken. This wasn’t the first documented event where Merkava tanks - the main tanks used in Gaza - were used against civilians since January 2022, when the bank’s Reputational Review committee supported the deal. Among the most high profile cases involving Merkava tanks include the siege on Gaza’s Al Shifa Hospital in November 2023 and the fatal attack on civilians waiting for food aid at the Al Tahliya roundabout, as the famine in Gaza worsened in June 2025. This was about nine months after the stated delivery date of the new Renk gearboxes and a month after the IDF published photos of the Renk gearboxes being prepared for mounting. Sufian Kawareh, 43, had no choice but to go to the relief aid distribution route east of Khan Yunis, in the southern Gaza Strip, to wait among the crowds for trucks loaded with flour. At the “Al-Tahliya” roundabout—where Kawareh and thousands of starving people sat waiting for the trucks to arrive—shells fired from Israeli Merkava tanks struck the area. Kawareh felt “an iron saw cutting through his leg” and soon collapsed. After a week of suffering, doctors amputated his foot to keep him alive. Khaled Walid, 40, who was injured in the Al Tahliya incident, recalled a Merkava 4 tank shooting at the crowd. It was easily distinguishable from other tanks used by the Israeli army, he said. “It had a turret, a cannon, a machine gun and metal structures surrounding its body,” he said in an interview. Palestinian authorities said at least 59 people who had been waiting for aid were killed in the incident. The IDF said a crowd had gathered near a stuck aid truck close to its troops, that the details were under review, and that it “regrets any harm to uninvolved individuals. Nasser Medical Complex, the hospital that treated victims of the Al Tahliya roundabout attack, itself came under shelling from a Merkava tank a couple of months later, on Aug 25, 2025, killing Reuters journalist Husam al-Masri. When rescue workers and journalists rushed to the scene, the same tank returned and shelled the hospital again, according to eyewitness and journalist Osama Hisham, whose tent was opposite the Nasser Medical Complex. IDF officials cited by Israeli media at the time also said the same tank had fired twice. A total 22 Palestinians, including five journalists, some from Reuters and the Associated Press, rescue workers, and a health worker, were killed. The next day, the IDF said it was targeting a camera used by Hamas, but Reuters confirmed the camera belonged to the news agency. Shown photos of the shells from this incident during an interview, explosives engineer Mohamed Salem, who has experience in explosives disposal in conflict zones, confirmed the attack was the result of 120 mm artillery ammunition designed for the smooth bore guns of the Merkava tanks. The standard marking “CRTG 120” is visible on the projectile wall. Several of the high profile incidents involving the Merkava 4 happened before the first batch of supply supported by Deutsche Bank, was scheduled to be delivered in September 2024. According to our information, the incidents in Gaza did not affect the Deutsche Bank-Renk deal. The Merkava 4, the mainstay of Israel’s tank fleet, has played a significant role in ground operations inside Gaza since October 2023. According to Alwan Al-Abousi, an expert interviewed by Daraj media, its primary armament is a 120-mm smoothbore cannon that fires shells and laser-guided missiles, and is equipped with three 7.62-mm machine guns on the roof, in addition to a 60-mm grenade launcher; it has a maximum speed of 64 km/h and a range of 500 km. According to Al-Abousi, the most important feature of the Merkava 4 tank is its protection system for detecting anti-armor missiles, called “Trophy”, which fires a projectile to detonate them before they reach the tank. “Merkava 4 Main Battle Tanks (MBTs), being the most advanced variant, are typically fielded by active Armored Brigades of the Armored Corps of the IDF - the 7th, 188th and 401st Brigades. Merkava 3 MBTs are typically deployed by one of seven reserve Armored Brigades or with a reserve Company of three Companies making up an Armoured Battalion,” explained Leone Hadavi, a senior arms and weapons specialist working as an open source investigator internationally. In Gaza, this tank operated as part of armored formations working in coordination with infantry, engineering, reconnaissance, and aviation units. Its primary role was to provide direct fire support to advancing Israeli forces, protect attacking units in residential areas, breach Hamas and allied groups’ defenses, and engage positions firing on Israeli forces. However, the war has also revealed that the tank’s technical superiority does not make it immune to losses, particularly when operating in a complex urban environment and under threats from multiple directions, according to Abbousi. When contacted on various defence deals including the one involving Merkava 4 gearboxes, the bank said that it does not comment on specific clients or transactions and assesses defence sector businesses “on a case-by-case basis in accordance with applicable laws and internal guidelines”. “The review considers, among other factors, the goods and their intended purpose, end users, the situation in the recipient country, including any armed conflict, and relevant human rights and reputational risks. Where heightened concerns are identified, the bank applies enhanced due diligence and may decline a transaction where the risks cannot be appropriately mitigated.” Inside Deutsche Bank: Secrets, scandals and double standards of global financial giant exposed by leak Negative press In the December 2021 internal Reputational Risk memo, it was noted that given a rise in Israel-Palestine and Israel-Lebanon tensions across that year, “including cross-border strikes and violent treatment of protestors,” the deal was not without risk. However, declining such a deal might also invite “negative press” for the bank, given the “historic relationship of Germany and Israel”. “If non-participation becomes public, we could face criticism from media/government that we deny necessary support to Israel to allow its self-defense,” the memo reads. “Former Chancellor Angela Merkel just stated during her last visit to Israel in Oct. 2021 that the security of Israel is part of our “reason of state” and Germany is not neutral regarding the question of Israel’s security.” Every Deutsche Bank department consulted in the review said that on balance, the deal should go ahead. As the violence escalated in Gaza, Deutsche Bank remained committed to Renk. On Feb 7, 2024, when Renk went public on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, Deutsche Bank acted as one of the coordinators of its Initial Public Offering alongside Citigroup, Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan. Court case One of the justifications given by Deutsche Bank to support the Merkava 4 deal in 2022 was that the exports would still need to be approved by the German government. However, for most of 2024, hardly any export licences for Israel were approved in Germany, something that affected Renk and Rolls-Royce, who manufactured the Merkava 4 supply engines, sources familiar with the industry said. They said the supply issues jeopardised the Israeli ground offensive. Israel had ramped up its offensive significantly after the Hamas-led Oct 7, 2023 attack on South Israel that killed 1,200 people, including 815 civilians. In August 2025, the German government suspended the export of weapons to Israel. Around the same time, a regional appeals court in Hesse, Germany was considering a challenge brought by a Palestinian man in Gaza, who sought to halt German export licences for Renk tank transmission parts bound for Israel. He argued that the licences breached Germany’s constitutional duty to protect his right to life. A Frankfurt court had rejected his application in December 2024, finding he had no standing, and in September 2025 the appeals court upheld that ruling. Two months later, the German government lifted its partial military exports suspension to Israel, citing the ceasefire announced the month before. A year on, a UN inquiry found Israel continued committing “genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza”. Israel rejects this characterisation. More than 1,600 Palestinians - mostly civilians - have been killed in Israel attacks since the ceasefire. When contacted, Renk declined to comment. Rolls Royce declined to comment. A bomb made to penetrate forts Renk is not the only defence manufacturer whose products were used by the IDF against civilians, nor the only one supported by Deutsche Bank, posing a question on compliance with the bank’s own human rights policy. “Our principle is not to engage in any business activities where Deutsche Bank has substantiated evidence of material adverse human rights impacts and where it is determined through the bank's internal processes that such adverse human rights impacts cannot be avoided or appropriately mitigated,” the bank says in its statement on human rights. Another defence manufacturer with ties to Deutsche Bank is the Italian arms manufacturer Leonard S.p.a (partially State-owned). By October 2018, the bank was involved in a multi-million-euro Israel-related deal with Leonardo. The bank had been asked to issue trade-related guarantees to the Italian defence firm which was described internally as a “platinum client”. Leonardo produced the 76/62 Super Rapid Multi Feeding Naval Gun Mounts, a weapon that can fire 120 rounds a minute, for Israel’s Sa’ar 6-class corvettes–Israel’s newest and most advanced warships. The IDF has used these warships to shell Gaza from the sea since 2023. The 76/62 Super Rapid Multi Feeding Naval Gun Mounts were produced and delivered in a deal guaranteed by Deutsche Bank. Leonardo, via a subsidiary, also makes automatic loaders for the Trophy APS system that protects ground vehicles against potential attacks, including the Merkava 4. Leonardo is currently facing a lawsuit by a Palestinian citizen and several Italian advocacy groups, for breaching the Italian Constitution, by allegedly supplying weapons to Israel that were used to violate human rights. Leonardo, via a subsidiary, also makes automatic loaders for the Trophy APS system that protects ground vehicles against potential attacks, including the Merkava 4. Leonardo’s CEO last year refuted accusations that his company was complicit in the Gaza conflict. In a response to questions from Barracuda Media, the company acknowledged its relationship with Deutsche Bank. It said it has always operated in strict compliance with national and international regulations governing the export of defense equipment and dual-use goods, as well as in accordance with authorisations granted by the competent authorities. It noted that following the escalation of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, Italian authorities have suspended the issuance of new licenses for the export of defense equipment to Israel. In 2024, BankTrack and 18 other civil society organisations published a report detailing how commercial banks were financing companies that arm Israel weapons. Deutsche Bank, it found, had extended about EUR4 billion in loans and underwriting to defence manufacturers Boeing, Leonardo, Lockheed Martin, Rolls Royce, RTX Corp and General Dynamics between January 2021 and August 2023, although not all their products were used in Gaza. One of the bombs made by Boeing, with key components provided by the French MBDA, a joint venture 25% owned by Leonardo, is the GBU Small Diameter Bomb. The bomb was used by the IDF via its air force to strike homes and urban areas. According to two weapons experts who reviewed photos of the aftermath, it was likely used in the attack on the Al-Mutanabbi School near Khan Younis in July 2024 that claimed the lives of 29 Palestinians. Analysing photos of the aftermath of the attack, explosives engineer Muhammad Salem said bomb fragments seen at the scene certainly came from precision-guided bombs of the GBU-39 type, or to its fine suspension and control system, based on the serial number printed on the metal. The fragments also revealed the manufacturer code registered to Woodward Inc, one of the suppliers of electromechanical systems and guidance actuators for the Boeing. In addition, the numbers showed the exact manufacturing date of the part on March 31, 2022 (2022-03-31), Salem said. He added that the bomb was designed to penetrate forts. Arms expert Hadavi agrees. In photos of the aftermath, at least one of the GBU Small Diameter Bomb’s four tail-mounted control surfaces, or the “tail wing”, can be seen, he said. Boeing also makes the bigger and stronger GBU-31, which was dropped on displaced peoples in tents in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis on July 13, 2024. That attack left more than 300 injured and killed 91 Palestinians, according to statistics from the Palestinian Ministry of Health at the time. On November 12, 2026, the US-made 250-pound GBU-39/B bomb was used in an IDF airstrike against Nasser Medical Complex, killing at least six people including a child and prominent surgeon Dr Rizk Abu Shaira, and wounding 52 others. In a statement, the IDF said it was targeting Hamas militants hiding inside the hospital but Hamas denied this. Since Oct 7, 2023, Israel has killed more than 75,000 people in Palestine and more than 3,000 in South Lebanon. The deaths include hundreds of journalists and aid workers, more than 1,700 healthcare workers and medical personnel and at least 20,000 children. According to a UN inquiry, children were deliberately targeted “using quadcopters, drones, and sniper rifles…to their head and upper body”. BankTrack’s human rights lead Ryan Brightwell said that financial institutions have clear human rights responsibilities. “They need to show how they respect human rights and they're expected to use their leverage over clients to ensure that they're not causing or contributing to harms,” he said. If a bank engages with an arms company, “it should be considering divesting or ending the relationship if the client doesn't change its behavior,” he added. Boeing, RTX Corp and General Dynamics did not respond to our questions. In a statement, Lockheed Martin said: “We continue to advance global security through technologies that enable the defense forces of our primary customers, the U.S. Government and its allies, to promote deterrence and defend human rights by adhering to U.S. Government oversight and policy objectives for all international sales.” The company also referred reporters to its online statement on human rights. Controversial weapons In March 2019, Deutsche Bank expanded its defence policy, which it said “makes clear” it would avoid “entering into, or continuing, any kind of business relationship” with entities that have “clear, direct links” to controversial weapons. Controversial weapons policies “can include landmines, cluster munitions, nuclear weapons or any kind of weapons that are likely to cause indiscriminate harm. And white phosphorus would clearly fall into that bracket,” said Bank Track’s Brightwell. White phosphorus is known for setting buildings on fire and burning flesh to bone. As of June 30, 2026, the bank owns 0.14% of ICL Group, a white phosphorus supplier, through shares worth US$8.98 million. It also held Israel Chemical Ltd (ICL) bonds as late as August 2019, months after its policy expansion. Two ICL subsidiaries, ICL Performance Products and ICL-IP Americahave supplied white phosphorus to a US Army plant in Arkansas that fills artillery shells, on multiple occasions since 2008, according to published Army contracts. The Washington Post and Amnesty International have reported that shells from that plant were exported to Israel. Since 2023, the IDF has deployed projectile artillery made with white phosphorus in Gaza and South Lebanon more than a dozen times, HRW reported. Deutsche Bank internal correspondence suggest how the bank could be employing a loophole in its own policy, by differentiating a parent company and wholly-owned subsidiaries, when defining “direct links” to companies involved in the production and supply of controversial weapons. In December 2019, a Deutsche Bank reputational risk officer in London told colleagues that transactions involving multinational giant Bayer Group, did not have to be flagged for controversial weapons. Instead, only transactions involving Monsanto Co, a fully-owned Bayer subsidiary, needed to be flagged. ICL provides phosphate to Monsanto for production of white phosphorus, later used to make munitions, according to arms trade watchdog Corruption Tracker. ICL, the Bayer Group, the IDF and Deutsche Bank did not respond to our questions on white phosphorus. A lucrative deal After spending about two decades researching global arms procurement, Andrew Feinstein believes that when it comes to defence deals, financial institutions are primarily motivated by only two things: profit and reputation. “They honestly don't care a damn about how many people might get killed, violations of international humanitarian law, war crimes [...] unless it's going to have an impact on their reputation,” said Feinstein, who is executive director of Shadow World Investigations, a UK-based non-profit investigating corruption in arms trade. At the operational level, he said, this could see bank officers clashing with often “junior” compliance officers, in order to secure their own annual bonuses. “If you’re generating a certain income [for the company], that is reflected in your annual bonus. So you're talking about people who are making decisions that are going to personally determine whether they personally make tens of thousands of euros or millions of euros at the end of that financial year,” he said in an interview. In January 2021, Deutsche Bank mulled over a potential lucrative deal with Israeli defence maker Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), even though the Israeli defence maker was off-boarded because it produced controversial weapons. IAI produced the Harpy in the 1980s, a drone which flies over battlefields searching for enemy radar signals before autonomously attacking the targets. The Harpy was one of the Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) flagged by the bank’s internal intelligence unit in April 2019, when the Industry Reputation Risk team considered developing a LAWS policy ahead of the bank’s AGM that year. In December 2019, an internal policy was put in place to exclude “human out of the loop” LAWS, the bank said. But in 2021, a senior corporate relationship manager for Central Europe and Israel pushed for IAI to get a second chance. One of the reasons: EUR 1.5 million in annual revenue. Undeterred, he sought senior management support. “We are currently working on a potential US$150 million AR business opportunity with the US$4.1 billion major defence manufacturer Israel Aerospace Industries Ltd. (IAI) as seller and Government of India / Agencies as obligors. The annual revenue potential of this transaction is EUR 1.5mn and additional AR business opportunities could arise later on,” he wrote to a head of trade finance. “We are reaching out to you to get your view as this is a sizable transaction and a sensible reputation risk topic, which would require senior management support in the reputation risk committees,” he said. He said the CEO of IAI had given assurances that the company was not involved in making controversial weapons and would not be doing so in the future. “We need to appeal the decision to a Regional Reputational Risk Committee and then to the Global Reputational Risk Committee,” he wrote to yet another trade finance specialist. IAI did not respond to requests for comment.
